title: Steam blocking crochet
subtitle: A light hover of steam relaxes the fabric and sets the shape
excerpt: Steam blocking is the fast finishing method for crochet. An iron held above the pinned piece releases steam, the fabric relaxes, the stitches even out, the shape sets. Quick, gentle on wool and cotton, the right choice for everyday pieces.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet, blocking chapter. Modern textile-care guidance from the Craft Yarn Council and the Hand Knitting Association.

glossaryTerms.definition: The finishing step where a finished crochet piece is pinned to shape and dampened (with steam, water, or spray) so the fibres relax and set in the desired shape.

heroPrompt: A finished crochet square pinned out flat on a foam blocking mat with rust-proof T-pins around the edges, a household iron held a few inches above with steam visibly rising — soft daylight, plain background.

content.text: Steam blocking is the fast finishing method for crochet. You pin the finished piece to a foam mat in the shape you want, hover a steam iron a few centimetres above without touching the fabric, and let the steam do the work. The fibres relax, the stitches even out, the shape sets.
Steam works well on wool and cotton. It is too aggressive for acrylic — the synthetic fibres can melt or permanently flatten. For acrylic pieces, use wet blocking or spray blocking instead.

attrs.title: What you need
attrs.body: A foam blocking mat (or a folded towel on the floor). Rust-proof blocking pins (standard sewing pins corrode and stain the yarn). A soft tape measure. A household steam iron with a working steam button. A spray bottle of cool water as a backup if the iron's steam is weak.

content.text: Fasten off and sew in all yarn tails before blocking. The blocking step sets the tails in place; loose tails after blocking are harder to bury.
Lay the foam mat on a flat surface. Place the finished piece face-up on the mat. Smooth it out gently — no stretching yet.

Pin the piece to the target shape and dimensions. Use the soft tape measure to check that the width and length match the pattern's quoted finished size. Pin every 5 cm along each edge for a square piece; closer (every 2 cm) on curves and corners.

Heat the steam iron to the wool setting (about 130°C). Hold the iron 2-3 cm above the fabric. Press the steam button. Move the iron slowly across the piece, releasing steam over each area for two or three seconds. Never touch the iron to the fabric — the heat scorches stitches and flattens the structure.

When the whole piece has been steamed, leave it pinned to the mat until completely cool and dry. This usually takes about 30 minutes. Removing the pins early lets the piece spring back to its unblocked shape.

Unpin and lift the piece off the mat. The shape should hold without springing back. If it springs back significantly, the steam wasn't dense enough — re-pin, re-steam more heavily, and leave for longer.

attrs.heading: When steam blocking goes wrong
attrs.intro: Four common steam blocking problems and the fix for each.

items.symptom: The piece is flattened, shiny, or stiff after blocking
items.cause: The iron touched the fabric. Steam blocks crochet; direct iron contact crushes the stitch structure permanently.
items.fix: There's no full fix once stitches are crushed. For minor crush damage on wool, a re-wet-block can plump the stitches back partway. Steam blocking is always done with the iron held above the fabric, never touching.

items.symptom: Acrylic yarn went limp or melted in patches
items.cause: Acrylic fibres can't handle steam. The synthetic doesn't relax like wool — it deforms.
items.fix: Use wet blocking or spray blocking for acrylic instead. The piece can't be recovered from steam damage on acrylic.

items.symptom: The pins left rust marks on the yarn
items.cause: Standard sewing pins or knitting pins corrode in steam.
items.fix: Use rust-proof T-pins or lace pins only. Mark the rust spots with a damp cloth; sometimes the stain comes out with a gentle hand-wash. Replace the pins with rust-proof ones for future blocking.

items.symptom: The piece won't stay in shape after unpinning
items.cause: Pins removed before the piece dried fully, or not enough steam used.
items.fix: Re-pin and steam-block again, holding the steam for longer. Leave pinned until completely dry — at least an hour for a thick piece. For pieces that resist blocking (densely-textured stitches), wet blocking gives a more permanent set than steam.

content.text: Steam works for most everyday pieces. Wet blocking gives a more permanent set on lace, doilies, and pieces with delicate stitch structure that need to open up — and it's the only method for acrylic. Spray blocking sits between the two and suits superwash wool. The blocking method is the finisher; the wrong method can undo a piece's quality.
